title: DRYLAB-Bench: Benchmarking the Biosecurity Risk of Agentic LLM Mutation Design
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

Title:DRYLAB-Bench: Benchmarking the Biosecurity Risk of Agentic LLM Mutation Design
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:As large language models (LLMs) acquire advanced biological design capabilities, they offer substantial research benefits but simultaneously introduce severe dual-use risks, such as engineering enhanced pathogens or drug-resistant bacteria. While biosecurity frameworks recognize these threats, the actual risk of LLMs executing dangerous biological modifications remains unquantified, particularly when augmented with specialized biological design tools (BDTs). Existing evaluations primarily assess hazardous knowledge possession rather than practical application, overlook risk amplification from BDTs, and rely on unreliable, expensive, or hazardous validation methods. To address these gaps, we introduce DRYLAB-Bench (Design Risk Yielded by LLM Agent in Biodesign), the first comprehensive benchmark evaluating the high-risk biological mutation design capabilities of LLM agents. Moving beyond basic question-answering, DRYLAB-Bench tasks agents with 30 genuinely hazardous mutation-design scenarios distilled from biosecurity guidelines. It evaluates models in a multi-round, tool-augmented environment where LLMs orchestrate BDTs to iteratively refine candidates. Crucially, it scores designs directly against 187,695 empirical wet-lab measurements from ProteinGym and ViroGym using our proposed Biosecurity Risk Score (BRS), quantifying risk-associated effects while enabling scalable and safe ground-truth verification. Evaluations of 15 frontier models reveal substantial baseline threats: without tools, 67.6% of one-shot designs exceed the average measured variant, and 21.4% reach the highest-risk decile. Equipping models with BDTs significantly amplifies this risk, raising the pooled risk by \(\Delta BRS=+0.116\) and the top-decile share to 23.5%. Code: this https URL

report.summary: New DRYLAB-Bench benchmark quantifies how LLM agents, especially with biological design tools, can design high-risk pathogen mutations, revealing notable dual-use biosecurity risks.
report.background: Large language models are increasingly capable in biological design, offering benefits for protein engineering, drug discovery, and synthetic biology. The same capabilities create dual-use risks: models could help design enhanced pathogens or drug-resistant bacteria. Existing biosecurity evaluations mostly test whether models possess hazardous knowledge through question-answering, not whether they can apply it in practice. They also ignore how specialized biological design tools (BDTs) can amplify an agent's capabilities. Validating actual risk is difficult because wet-lab testing is expensive, slow, and potentially dangerous. DRYLAB-Bench addresses these gaps by benchmarking the practical, agentic mutation-design capabilities of LLMs against large-scale empirical fitness data, providing a safer and more scalable way to quantify biosecurity risk.
key_points: DRYLAB-Bench is the first benchmark to evaluate agentic LLM biosecurity risk in mutation design, rather than simple knowledge recall. It presents 30 hazardous mutation-design scenarios drawn from biosecurity guidelines and runs models in a multi-round, tool-augmented environment where the agent orchestrates biological design tools to iteratively refine candidate mutations.

The benchmark scores designs against 187,695 wet-lab measurements from ProteinGym and ViroGym using a new Biosecurity Risk Score (BRS). This enables scalable, safe ground-truth verification without hazardous experiments, and quantifies risk-associated effects rather than just plausibility or knowledge.

Evaluating 15 frontier models reveals substantial baseline risk. Without tools, 67.6% of one-shot designs exceed the average measured variant, and 21.4% reach the highest-risk decile. This shows current models already produce dangerous mutation candidates zero-shot, before any tool augmentation.

Equipping models with biological design tools significantly amplifies risk. Pooled risk rises by ΔBRS = +0.116, and the share of designs in the top risk decile increases to 23.5%. Tool access thus acts as a risk multiplier, a factor prior evaluations largely overlooked.

The results highlight a gap between biosecurity policy and model capability. Benchmarks that only test knowledge miss practical, agentic misuse potential. DRYLAB-Bench offers a repeatable evaluation layer that regulators, model developers, and labs can use to assess and mitigate dual-use risk before deployment.
report.impact: The study pushes biosecurity evaluation from knowledge tests toward practical capability measurement, giving policymakers and model providers a concrete metric for dual-use risk. For the AI industry, it strengthens the case for capability-gated access to biological design tools, pre-deployment red-teaming, and safety training that targets agentic planning. Developers building bio-AI agents may face new expectations: refusal behaviors, tool-level usage caps, monitoring, and safer-by-design architectures. For regular users, the direct effect is limited, but the broader consequence is that frontier models may be governed more like high-consequence technologies, with restricted bio-related features or stronger verification. At the same time, the benchmark supports beneficial research by enabling safer evaluation of protein engineering and drug design models without real-world hazardous experiments.
report.tools: Follow the DRYLAB-Bench code release linked from the paper for evaluation harness details. Related resources include ProteinGym and ViroGym for empirical fitness data, plus biosecurity screening frameworks such as the Nucleic Acid Observatory and the International Biosecurity and Biosafety Initiative for Science. AI safety toolkits and open evaluation platforms like HELM Safety are also worth watching for agentic bio-risk assessments.
